claims.text: Brittle behavior in initially single-phase high-entropy alloys emerges from stress- and temperature-induced local compositional partitioning rather than bulk intermetallic precipitation.
Local compositional partitioning produces nanoscale segregation at grain boundaries.
Nanoscale grain-boundary segregation weakens intergranular cohesion.
Segregation-induced loss of grain-boundary cohesion reduces toughness under service exposure.
Preexistent grain-boundary phases dominate brittle behavior in conventional alloys.
The proposed initial material is a homogenized, single-phase compositionally complex high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has a uniform elemental distribution and no detectable grain-boundary segregation.
Combined elevated-temperature exposure and mechanical loading can induce grain-boundary segregation relative to benign conditions.
Under high-temperature and high-strain conditions, local diffusional processes promote segregation of constituent elements to grain boundaries.
Segregation can cause a transition from ductile to brittle fracture without conventional intermetallic precipitation.
Aggressively exposed specimens will develop localized grain-boundary compositional fluctuations detectable by atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM.
Aggressively exposed specimens will show reduced fracture toughness relative to the initial state and benign control.
The benign control will retain a uniform composition and high toughness.
The mechanism applies where thermal activation and mechanical stress permit segregation without full-scale phase decomposition or grain coarsening.
At lower temperatures or strain rates, the alloy retains its toughness.
